q-83391.name: Question 1
q-83391.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}],$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
q-83391.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-4)\cdot 7-(-5)\cdot 3 \\  & =-28+15 \\  & =-13.\end{aligned}
$$

q-40173.name: Question 11
q-40173.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}],$ and ${A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
q-40173.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-5A-2 & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-5A-2) & ={A}^{-1}O \\ A-5I-2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =-\frac{5}{2}I+\frac{1}{2}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\frac{5}{2},$ $q=\frac{1}{2}$ and

$$
p+q=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=-2.
$$

q-85930.name: Question 13
q-85930.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -3-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & -2 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((-3-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+2) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -1) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+5\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}-{A}^{3}+5A-2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}(-{A}^{3}+5A-2I) & =O \\ -{A}^{2}+5I-2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 2{A}^{-1} & =5I-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{5}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-37779.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
q-37779.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ 1 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(7-\lambda )+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+9I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+9I) & =O \\ A-8I+9{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{8}{9}I-\frac{1}{9}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{8}{9},$ $q=-\frac{1}{9},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{8}{9}+(-\frac{1}{9})=\frac{7}{9}.
$$

q-37775.problem: If $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}+x-2,$ then ${A}^{4}=$
q-37775.worked_solution:
First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{4}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}+x-2,$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{2}$ $-$ $x$ $+$ $3$
${x}^{2}+x-2\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{4}\phantom{|}\,\,\,}$
${x}^{4}$ $+$ ${x}^{3}$ $-$ $2{x}^{2}$
$-$ ${x}^{3}$ $+$ $2{x}^{2}$
$-$ ${x}^{3}$ $-$ ${x}^{2}$ $+$ $2x$
$3{x}^{2}$ $-$ $2x$
$3{x}^{2}$ $+$ $3x$ $-$ $6$
$-$ $5x$ $+$ $6$
Therefore, we can write ${x}^{4}$ as $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{4} & =q(x)p(x)+(-5x+6),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{2}-x+3.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ {A}^{4}=q(A)p(A)+(-5A+6I). $$ Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{4} & =q(A)p(A)+(-5A+6I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(-5A+6I) \\ & =-5A+6I.\end{aligned} $$
